answerBody:
Congress should hold S. 5653 rather than pass it, before the new Congress convenes, as the governing framework for data-center grid costs and energy buildout. The right posture is a narrower rewrite that keeps mandatory large-load cost allocation and transmission planning, while preserving the environmental, tribal, and judicial-review constraints the current substitute would cut.

The November 9, 2026 vote was cloture on the motion to proceed, 73 to 25, not final passage. Sponsors Shelley Moore Capito, Mike Lee, Sheldon Whitehouse, and Martin Heinrich are moving the package through a manager's amendment that the National Congress of American Indians described, on November 8, as a 494-page substitute to H.R. 2347. That text is not a data-center rate bill. It rewrites the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, and parts of the Federal Power Act, while expanding Federal Energy Regulatory Commission authority over interstate transmission.

The separable core is worth enacting. Senator Heinrich's Energy and Natural Resources fact sheet says the bill would require data centers to pay associated transmission costs rather than rely on a voluntary structure, so those costs are not shifted to households and small businesses. Stronger regional planning and a federal backstop for interstate lines address a real bottleneck. Those claims support speed on cost allocation and transmission, not freezing the rest.

NCAI urged a no vote and said the amendment left the structural harms intact. On its reading, courts could generally only remand Section 106 and NEPA violations without vacatur or an injunction, so construction could continue after an action was found unlawful. Agencies could end historic-preservation review in their sole discretion. Clocks of 30 and 45 days would treat consultation as fulfilled once an agency replied in writing, and the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation could still sign in lieu of a Tribal Historic Preservation Officer. NCAI also said there had been no hearing, markup, or meaningful tribal consultation. Those changes would reset the legal baseline far beyond data centers and are hard to unwind once signed.

The strongest case for passage now is coalition fragility. A 73-vote cloture may not reassemble if chairs or control change in January, and waiting could leave households socializing data-center grid costs. That risk is more reversible. Cost allocation can be reenacted, and FERC can move on rates without this statute. A lame-duck bar on vacatur and injunctive relief would govern later challenges unrelated to computing load. Cloture on a motion to proceed is not consent to that remedy structure.

This review did not include a page-by-page reading of the substitute or a score separating ratepayer savings from the judicial-review title. That gap does not favor treating the current text as the framework. If sponsors strip remand-without-vacatur, sole-discretion Section 106 off-ramps, and deemed consultation before final passage, a narrow lame-duck bill is appropriate. If not, Congress should hold the package and rewrite it with Tribal Nations at the table.
rationale: Hold S. 5653 for a narrower rewrite. The November 9 cloture was procedural, not final passage, and the package rewrites NEPA, CWA, ESA, NHPA Section 106, and parts of the Federal Power Act rather than only allocating data-center grid costs. Heinrich's fact sheet supports mandatory large-load cost allocation and transmission planning, but NCAI's November 8 statement says the manager's amendment still limits remedies to remand without vacatur or injunction, allows sole-discretion Section 106 off-ramps, and deems consultation fulfilled on short clocks. Coalition fragility is the strongest counterargument, but cost allocation is more reversible than those judicial and tribal constraints.
